newsitem.title: GERMANY: German SPD leader signals compromise in tax debate.
newsitem.headline: German SPD leader signals compromise in tax debate.

text.p: As his party trades accusations with Germany's ruling coalition over an ambitious tax reform plan, a senior opposition Social Democrat signalled interest in reaching a compromise at talks this week.

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of Lower Saxony and considered the opposition's prime candidate to topple Chancellor Helmut Kohl in next autumn's elections, urged the SPD to reach a compromise with Kohl's Christian Democrats and junior coalition partner Free Democrats, the German newspaper Welt am Sonntag said.

Eager to avoid having his party labelled a reform-blocking nay-sayer, Schroeder suggested the SPD should largely agree to Bonn's plans as long as the coalition backed off proposals to tax wages earned on weekends, the newspaper reported.

At issue is Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut 30 billion marks ($17.5 billion) in taxes designed to increase investment and cut high unemployment. The tax reform's timing is critical as the government scrambles to trim its budget deficit to meet entry criteria for European monetary union.
But the SPD can block most tax measures through its control of the upper house of parliament.
The two sides are scheduled to meet again on Wednesday after making little progress at talks last Tuesday.
Wolfgang Gerhard, leader of the Free Democrats, on Sunday warned the FDP would not allow the SPD to wreck the tax reform concept by simply shifting around the tax burden.
"If the Social Democrats on Wednesday again oppose a reduction in taxes, then further talks would be a waste of time," Gerhard was quoted as saying by Welt am Sonntag.

As part of its demands, the SPD wants the government to cut labour insurance charges by two percentage points from July to improve job prospects. The government agreed to make a one-point cut, but only if the SPD gives its full backing to its tax plans.
Waigel also says the reduction should go hand-in-hand with reforms to state pensions, health and jobless schemes.

While Schroeder appeared more conciliatory, SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine attacked Bonn's plans, saying they would create an annual financing gap of 56 billion marks ($32.5 billion) which would have to be paid by state and local governments.
"None of the 16 German states can absorb such deficits. For the east German states, the Kohl government's tax plans are a catastrophe," Lafontaine wrote in the Leipziger Volkszeitung.

On Sunday in Bonn, Lafontaine suggested that each side's demands should be broken down into separate issues, saying a reform taken in steps would be better than no reform at all. Christian Wulff, the Christian Democrat leader in the state of Lower Saxony, however urged the government to stick by its plans and not give in to the SPD's "tactical demands".

"To follow Lafontaine's wish and first negotiate new tax increases and increased expenditures and later possibly discuss the larger tax reform would be a catastrophe," Wulff wrote in an opinion piece in Bild am Sonntag.

As part of a possible compromise, Welt am Sonntag reported plans were being made in Bonn to raise Germany's mineral oil tax from July 1. The newspaper quoted SPD member Helmut Wieczorek as saying, "the SPD would go along with that."
Waigel said two weeks ago he would be willing to cut social scurity contributions by about one point and finance this by raising indirect taxes.
But Bavaria premier Edmund Stoiber, a member of Waigel's Christian Social Union, rejected suggestions of a mineral oil tax increase, saying such a move would hurt the economy.

Instead Stoiber, in an interview in the magazine Focus, proposed: "An increase in VAT to offset a cut in social security contributions would improve our competitiveness and improve job security because labour would become cheaper."
